title: Unit 13: Geometric Optics

guide.title: Geometric optics: review guide
guide.intro: Geometric optics treats light as rays that travel in straight lines until they reflect, refract, or are absorbed. Mirrors and lenses use these rules to form images.
guide.equationNote: Sign convention used here: object and image distances are positive for real objects and real images; a virtual image has a negative image distance. Converging mirrors and lenses have positive focal lengths, and diverging ones have negative focal lengths. c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

sections.title: Reflection, refraction, and absorption
body: At a smooth surface, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured from the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface).

When light enters a different material it changes speed and bends: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, where n = c/v is the index of refraction. Going into a material with a larger n, light slows down and bends toward the normal.
points: Total internal reflection: going from a larger n to a smaller n, light that meets the boundary at more than the critical angle (sin θ_c = n₂/n₁) does not leave at all.
Materials absorb some wavelengths and reflect or transmit others; the color you see is the light that is not absorbed.
The frequency of light does not change when it enters a new material; its speed and wavelength do.
equations: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂

sections.title: Images from mirrors
body: A plane mirror forms a virtual, upright image the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.

Curved mirrors follow 1/s_o + 1/s_i = 1/f, with magnification M = −s_i/s_o = h_i/h_o. A concave (converging) mirror forms a real, inverted image when the object is beyond the focal point. A convex (diverging) mirror always forms a virtual, upright, smaller image.
points: For a spherical mirror, f = R/2.
A negative magnification means an inverted image; |M| > 1 means an enlarged image.
Check with a ray diagram: a ray parallel to the axis reflects through the focal point of a concave mirror, or as if from the focal point of a convex mirror.

sections.title: Images from lenses
body: A converging (convex) lens brings parallel rays together at its focal point; a diverging (concave) lens spreads them out as if they came from its focal point. The same equation, 1/s_o + 1/s_i = 1/f, applies.

With a converging lens, an object beyond f gives a real, inverted image on the far side; an object inside f gives a virtual, upright, enlarged image, which is how a magnifying glass works. A diverging lens always gives a virtual, upright, smaller image.
points: An object at 2f forms a real, inverted image at 2f, the same size as the object.
An object exactly at f forms no image: the rays leave parallel.
A lens's focal length depends on its shape and on how its index of refraction compares with its surroundings.

example.prompt: An object is 12 cm from a converging lens with f = 8.0 cm. Find the image distance and the magnification.
example.solution: 1/s_i = 1/8.0 − 1/12 = 1/24, so s_i = 24 cm: a real image on the far side of the lens. M = −24/12 = −2.0, so the image is inverted and twice as tall as the object.

misconceptions: “Light bends away from the normal when it enters glass.”
Entering a material with a larger index of refraction, it slows down and bends toward the normal.
“A mirror's image is on the mirror's surface.”
A plane mirror's image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
“Covering half a lens cuts off half the image.”
Every part of the lens forms the whole image; covering half only makes it dimmer.
“A virtual image can be shown on a screen.”
Only a real image, where light actually comes together, can be projected onto a screen.

questions.prompt: A light ray strikes a flat mirror at 35° from the normal. At what angle from the normal does it reflect?
questions.explanation: The law of reflection: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured from the normal. So the ray reflects at 35°.
choiceExplanations: 55° is the angle from the mirror's surface; both angles are measured from the normal.
70° is the angle between the incoming and reflected rays, not the angle of reflection.
145° is 180° − 35°; the reflected ray leaves at the same angle from the normal as it arrived.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and official topics come from the linked College Board page, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-10-09); that page was used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: Light in air (n = 1.00) strikes a glass surface (n = 1.50) at 60° from the normal. At about what angle from the normal does it travel in the glass?
questions.explanation: Snell's law: sin θ₂ = (1.00)(sin 60°)/1.50 = 0.866/1.50 = 0.577, so θ₂ ≈ 35°. The light bends toward the normal as it slows down.
choiceExplanations: 40° divides the angle itself by 1.50; Snell's law relates the sines of the angles.
60° would mean no bending, but light changes direction when it changes speed.
55° is the angle from the surface (90° − 35°); angles are measured from the normal.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and official topics come from the linked College Board page, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-10-09); that page was used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: Light travels from a vacuum into water, which has an index of refraction of 1.33. What is its speed in the water? (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)
choiceExplanations: 4.0 × 10⁸ m/s multiplies by n; light is slower in water, not faster.
3.0 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed in a vacuum; an index above 1 means light is slower.
4.4 × 10⁻⁹ is n/c, the ratio upside down.

questions.prompt: Light inside a block of glass (n = 1.50) meets the glass–air boundary at 45° from the normal. What happens?
choices: It is totally reflected back into the glass, because 45° is larger than the critical angle of about 42°
It passes into the air, bending toward the normal
It passes into the air, bending away from the normal, at about 64°
It passes straight into the air without bending
questions.explanation: The critical angle is given by sin θ_c = 1.00/1.50, so θ_c ≈ 41.8°. Since 45° is larger, Snell's law would need sin θ₂ = 1.50 × sin 45° ≈ 1.06, which is impossible, so all the light reflects.
choiceExplanations: Going into air (smaller n), light would bend away from the normal, and here it cannot leave at all.
No refracted angle exists: 1.50 × sin 45° ≈ 1.06 is greater than 1, so no light leaves the glass.
Light bends at any boundary it meets at an angle; here, beyond the critical angle, none of it leaves.

questions.prompt: Why does a leaf look green in white light?
choices: It absorbs most other colors and reflects mostly green light
It absorbs mostly green light and reflects the rest
It creates green light from the white light
It slows green light down more than other colors
questions.explanation: White light contains all colors. The leaf absorbs much of the red and blue light and reflects mostly green, so green light reaches your eyes.
choiceExplanations: The color you see is the light that is reflected, not the light that is absorbed.
The leaf does not create light; it removes some colors from the white light by absorbing them.
The leaf's color comes from absorption and reflection, not from light slowing down inside it.

questions.prompt: You stand 2.0 m in front of a flat (plane) mirror. Where is your image, and what is it like?
choices: 2.0 m behind the mirror: virtual, upright, and the same size
On the surface of the mirror: virtual and upright
2.0 m in front of the mirror: real and inverted
4.0 m behind the mirror: virtual and half the size
questions.explanation: A plane mirror forms a virtual image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, upright and the same size.
choiceExplanations: The image appears behind the mirror, not on its surface.
A plane mirror cannot form a real image; reflected rays only appear to come from behind it.
4.0 m is the distance from you to your image; the image is 2.0 m behind the mirror and the same size as you.

questions.prompt: An object is 30 cm in front of a concave mirror with a focal length of 10 cm. Where is the image, and what is it like?
choices: 15 cm in front of the mirror: real, inverted, and half the size
15 cm behind the mirror: virtual, upright, and half the size
7.5 cm in front of the mirror: real and inverted
20 cm in front of the mirror: real and inverted
questions.explanation: 1/s_i = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30, so s_i = +15 cm: a real image in front of the mirror. M = −15/30 = −0.5, so it is inverted and half the size.
choiceExplanations: A positive image distance means the image is in front of the mirror, where it is real; virtual images have negative s_i.
7.5 cm adds 1/10 + 1/30 instead of subtracting 1/30.
20 cm subtracts the distances (30 − 10); the mirror equation uses reciprocals.

questions.prompt: An object is 20 cm in front of a convex mirror with a focal length of −20 cm. Where is the image, and what is it like?
choices: 10 cm behind the mirror: virtual, upright, and half the size
No image forms, because the object is at the focal length
10 cm in front of the mirror: real and inverted
20 cm behind the mirror: virtual, upright, and the same size
questions.explanation: 1/s_i = 1/f − 1/s_o = −1/20 − 1/20 = −1/10, so s_i = −10 cm: a virtual image 10 cm behind the mirror. M = −(−10)/20 = +0.5: upright and half the size.
choiceExplanations: That happens for a concave mirror with the object at its focal point. A convex mirror's focal point is behind it, so an image always forms.
A convex mirror always forms a virtual image; the negative s_i puts it behind the mirror.
Same distance and same size describes a plane mirror; a convex mirror makes images smaller and closer.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and official topics come from the linked College Board page, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-10-09); that page was used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: An object is 3.0 cm from a converging lens with a focal length of 5.0 cm, as with a magnifying glass. What image forms?
choices: A virtual, upright image 2.5 times as tall, 7.5 cm from the lens on the object's side
A real, inverted image 7.5 cm from the lens on the other side
A real image 1.9 cm from the lens
No image, because the object is inside the focal length
questions.explanation: 1/s_i = 1/5.0 − 1/3.0 = −2/15, so s_i = −7.5 cm: a virtual image on the same side as the object. M = −(−7.5)/3.0 = +2.5: upright and 2.5 times as tall.
choiceExplanations: The negative image distance means the image is virtual and on the object's side, not real on the far side.
1.9 cm adds 1/5.0 + 1/3.0 instead of subtracting.
An object inside the focal length gives a virtual, enlarged image; that is how a magnifying glass works.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and official topics come from the linked College Board page, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-10-09); that page was used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: An object is 20 cm from a converging lens with a focal length of 10 cm. How far from the lens is the image?
choices: 20 cm
10 cm
6.7 cm
30 cm
questions.explanation: 1/s_i = 1/10 − 1/20 = 1/20, so s_i = 20 cm. An object at 2f forms a real, inverted, same-size image at 2f.
choiceExplanations: 10 cm is the focal length; only an object very far away forms its image at f.
6.7 cm adds 1/10 + 1/20 instead of subtracting.
30 cm adds the distances; the lens equation uses reciprocals.

questions.prompt: An object is 30 cm from a diverging lens with a focal length of −15 cm. What image forms?
choices: A virtual, upright image one third as tall, 10 cm from the lens on the object's side
A real, inverted image 30 cm from the lens
A virtual, upright image three times as tall
No image, because a diverging lens spreads the light out
questions.explanation: 1/s_i = −1/15 − 1/30 = −3/30, so s_i = −10 cm: a virtual image on the object's side. M = −(−10)/30 = +1/3: upright and one third as tall.
choiceExplanations: A diverging lens cannot form a real image of a real object.
A diverging lens makes images smaller, not larger: M = 1/3.
The spreading rays appear to come from a point on the object's side, which is the virtual image.
